is.je: the standard word for "is" used in normal statements
is.jeste: an emphatic form used to stress that something really is true
is.jel: a shortened question form (from je li) used to ask yes/no questions like “Is he…?”.

that.da: used to link two clauses (like “I know that…”)
that.taj: a demonstrative for “that” when pointing to something nearby and masculine
that.tog: the genitive form of taj used for possession or after prepositions
that.onaj: used for something more distant or specific (“that one over there”)
that.onoga: the genitive of onaj when the object is being affected.

are.su: the actual word for “are” used in plural subjects like “they are”
are.se: a reflexive marker that changes the verb’s meaning to reflexive or passive, not a direct translation of “are” but often paired with it.

and.i: the basic word for “and” that connects similar things
and.a: a contrastive version used like “but” or “while” to show difference
and.pa: used to show consequence or continuation, like “and then” or “so”.

in.u: the standard preposition used before a noun to say “in” (like “in the house”)
in.unutra: an adverb meaning “inside”, typically used to describe location or motion (“go inside”).

it.to: the most common neutral word for "it" when referring to something general or previously mentioned
it.ono: also means “it” but refers to a more distant or abstract thing, often something already known or obvious in context.

alone.samog: genitive or accusative masculine form used when the subject is being acted upon (e.g. “vidim samog čovjeka”)
alone.samoga: a formal or emphatic variant of samog, used more in writing or emphasis.

what.što: standard word for "what" in both questions and statements
what.šta: more colloquial and common in speech (especially in Bosnia and Serbia)
what.kakav: means “what kind of” or “what type”, used for descriptions
what.sta: variant spelling of šta (often dialectal or typographic)
what.če: not standard Croatian (likely typo or regional/dialectal)
what.kaj: regional (Zagorje, Northern Croatia) word for “what” used instead of što or šta.

on.na: means “on” in the physical sense (e.g. “on the table”)
on.o: means “about” or “concerning” (e.g. “pričamo o tebi” = “we’re talking about you”).

you.te: informal singular object pronoun (“I see you”)
you.tebe: emphatic or accusative form of “you” (e.g. “volim tebe”)
you.tobom: instrumental form meaning “with you” (e.g. “idem s tobom”)
you.vama: dative or instrumental plural/formal form of “you” (e.g. “dajem vama poklon”).

me.mi: dative form meaning “to me” (e.g. “daj mi knjigu” = “give me the book”)
me.mene: emphatic or accusative form used when “me” is the object (e.g. “voli mene, ne nju”)
me.mnom: instrumental form meaning “with me” (e.g. “idi sa mnom” = “go with me”).

you are.si: informal singular form (e.g. “ti si moj prijatelj”)
you are.ste: formal or plural form (e.g. “vi ste iz Zagreba”)
you are.jesi: emphatic or interrogative form of si (e.g. “jesi li gladan?” = “are you hungry?”).

but.ali: the standard word for “but”, used in all kinds of contrastive sentences
but.no: a slightly more formal or softer alternative, often used at the start of a sentence or as a transition (e.g. “No, to nije istina”).

with.s: means “with” and is used before words that don’t start with “s” or “š”
with.sa: also means “with” but is used before words starting with “s” or “š” to make pronunciation easier (e.g. “s tobom” but “sa svima”)
with.uz: means “along with” or “next to” and is used when expressing physical closeness or accompaniment in motion.

only.samo: the most common word for “only”, meaning “just” or “merely” in most situations (e.g. “samo gledam”)
only.jedini: means “the only one” as in “sole” or “unique” (e.g. “on je jedini prijatelj”)
only.tek: means “only” in the sense of “not until” or “just now” (e.g. “tek sam došao” = “I just arrived”).

him.ga: accusative form meaning “him” (e.g. “vidim ga” = “I see him”)
him.mu: dative form meaning “to him” (e.g. “daj mu knjigu” = “give him the book”)
him.njega: emphatic form of ga, used for contrast or emphasis (e.g. “ne njega, nego tebe”)
him.njim: instrumental form meaning “with him” (e.g. “pričam s njim”)
him.njemu: dative emphatic form (e.g. “njemu to ne smeta” = “he doesn’t mind that”).

this.ovo: neutral form meaning “this thing” or “this here”
this.ovaj: masculine form used before masculine nouns (e.g. “ovaj auto”)
this.ta: feminine demonstrative that can mean “that” or “this” depending on context (often older or poetic usage)
this.ovim: instrumental form used when “by this” or “with this” is meant (e.g. “ovim putem” = “by this way”).

will.će: the auxiliary verb used to form the future tense (e.g. “on će doći” = “he will come”)
will.hoće: full verb form of “will/wants” that can be used alone or in questions (e.g. “hoće li doći?”)
will.ce: incorrect spelling or unaccented form of će
will.volje: genitive or plural form of volja, which means “will” as in personal willpower
will.volja: the noun for “will” in the sense of desire or intent (e.g. “imam volju za to” = “I have the will for it”).

good.dobro: neutral form, used for general statements or as an adverb (e.g. “to je dobro” = “that’s good”)
good.dobar: masculine form used with masculine nouns (e.g. “dobar čovjek” = “a good man”)
good.dobrog: genitive or accusative masculine form (e.g. “vidim dobrog psa” = “I see the good dog”)
good.dobrim: instrumental masculine form (e.g. “s dobrim prijateljem” = “with a good friend”)
good.dobroj: dative or locative feminine form (e.g. “pričam dobroj osobi” = “I’m talking to a good person”).

if.ako: the standard word for “if”, used in most conditional sentences (e.g. “ako dođeš, javim se” = “if you come, I’ll let you know”)
if.ukoliko: a more formal or conditional version of ako, often used in writing or polite speech (e.g. “ukoliko bude problema, javite se”).

we are.smo: standard form for “we are”, placed after the subject (e.g. “mi smo spremni”)
we are.jesmo: emphatic version of smo used to affirm or contrast (e.g. “Jesmo, stigli smo!” = “Yes, we did arrive!”).

all.sve: neuter form or used as a general “everything” (e.g. “sve je gotovo” = “everything is done”)
all.svi: masculine plural meaning “everyone” or “all people” (e.g. “svi su tu”)
all.sva: feminine or neuter plural for “all things” depending on gender (e.g. “sva djeca” = “all children”)
all.sav: masculine singular meaning “all of” (e.g. “sav trud” = “all the effort”)
all.svu: accusative feminine singular (e.g. “vidim svu vodu” = “I see all the water”).

i will.ću: the auxiliary form meaning “I will”, used after the verb goes first (e.g. “napisat ću” = “I will write”)
i will.hoću: full form meaning both “I want” and “I will” (e.g. “hoću jesti” = “I want to eat” or “I will eat”), cu and hocu: incorrect/unaccented spellings of ću and hoću, often used in informal writing like texting but not correct in standard usage.

be.biti: the infinitive form “to be”, used in general or future constructions (e.g. “želim biti učitelj” = “I want to be a teacher”)
be.bude: third-person singular present or subjunctive form meaning “that it be” or “let it be” (e.g. “neka bude tako” = “let it be so”)
be.budi: imperative singular form meaning “be!” used for commands (e.g. “budi miran!” = “be quiet!”)
be.budite: formal or plural version of budi (e.g. “budite spremni” = “be ready”).

i know.znam: the most common form meaning “I know” (facts, skills, people casually)
i know.poznajem: used when you are familiar with someone/something personally, especially people or places (e.g. “poznajem tog čovjeka” = “I know that man”)
i know.poznám: an alternative (more common in some dialects or Serbian), used like poznajem, though in Croatian poznajem is preferred.

here.ovdje: standard, precise word for “here” (e.g. “on je ovdje” = “he is here”)
here.tu: more casual or general version of “here”, often interchangeable with ovdje but slightly more vague (e.g. “sjedni tu”)
here.evo: used to introduce or present something (e.g. “evo ga!” = “here it is!”)
here.ovamo: means “toward here” or “come this way” (e.g. “dođi ovamo”)
here.ovde: regional form used in Serbia and parts of Bosnia, equivalent to ovdje in standard Croatian.

was.bio: masculine singular past tense of “to be” (e.g. “on je bio tamo” = “he was there”)
was.bila: feminine singular past (e.g. “ona je bila sretna”)
was.bile: feminine plural past (e.g. “one su bile gladne”)
was.biio: misspelling or typo of bio — not standard.

i can.mogu: standard present tense form meaning “I can” (e.g. “mogu ti pomoći” = “I can help you”)
i can.moga: a past or conditional form meaning “could” or “might have” (e.g. “moga sam doći” = “I could have come”), although the full form is typically mogao in standard masculine singular.

why.zašto: the standard and most commonly used word for “why” in questions (e.g. “zašto kasniš?” = “why are you late?”)
why.čemu: literally means “to what purpose” or “for what”, used in more formal or rhetorical questions (e.g. “čemu to vodi?” = “what’s the point of that?”)
why.zasto: a misspelling or unaccented version of zašto, often seen in casual texting but not correct in standard Croatian.

more.još: means “more” in the sense of “still” or “additional” (e.g. “želim još vode” = “I want more water”)
more.više: comparative form meaning “more” as in greater quantity or degree (e.g. “više vremena” = “more time”)
more.vise: misspelling of više or the verb “to hang” depending on context — not interchangeable with više when meaning “more”.

something.nešto: the standard and most common word for “something” (e.g. “želim nešto slatko” = “I want something sweet”)
something.nesto: misspelling or unaccented form of nešto, often seen in texts
something.nečega: genitive form of “something” (e.g. “bojim se nečega” = “I’m afraid of something”)
something.nečemu: dative form, “to something” (e.g. “pristupiti nečemu” = “to approach something”)
something.nečim: instrumental form, “with something” (e.g. “bavi se nečim čudnim” = “he’s involved in something strange”), nečeg and nečem: shortened genitive/dative forms (used mostly in speech or poetry)
something.ponešto: means “somewhat” or “a bit of something” (e.g. “znam ponešto o tome” = “I know a bit about that”).

when.kad: informal or shortened form of kada, often used in speech (e.g. “kad dolaziš?”)
when.kada: the full and slightly more formal version of “when” used interchangeably with kad, especially in writing or careful speech.

who.koji: means “who” or “which” when selecting from a group or specifying (e.g. “koji čovjek?” = “which man?”)
who.tko: the standard Croatian word for “who” (e.g. “tko je to?” = “who is that?”)
who.koja: feminine form of koji, meaning “which” or “who” when referring to a feminine noun (e.g. “koja djevojka?”)
who.ko: a common colloquial or regional form of tko (used more in speech or outside standard grammar)
who.kog: genitive/accusative form of tko or koji, meaning “whom” or “of whom” (e.g. “kog si vidio?” = “whom did you see?”).

your.vas: accusative form of the plural/formal “you” (used as object, e.g. “čekam vas” = “I’m waiting for you”)
your.tvoj: masculine singular informal form of “your” (e.g. “tvoj auto”)
your.vaš: masculine singular formal or plural “your” (e.g. “vaš prijatelj”)
your.vaše: neuter or plural form (e.g. “vaše dijete” or “vaše stvari”)

i think.mislim: most commonly used verb for “I think” in the sense of “I believe” or “I suppose” (e.g. “mislim da je dobro”)
i think.smatram: more formal, meaning “I consider” or “I deem” (e.g. “smatram to važnim”)
i think.razmislim: means “I think it over” or “I reflect” — used for deliberate, thoughtful consideration (e.g. “moram razmisliti”)
i think.pomislim: used for a sudden or brief thought (e.g. “pomislim na njega” = “I suddenly think of him”).

thanks.hvala: the standard and universally used word for “thanks” or “thank you” in any context (e.g. “hvala puno”)
thanks.zahvaljujući: a preposition meaning “thanks to” (e.g. “zahvaljujući tebi, uspjeli smo” = “thanks to you, we succeeded”) — not used as a stand-alone thank-you.

them.ih: accusative form meaning “them” (e.g. “vidim ih” = “I see them”)
them.im: dative form meaning “to them” (e.g. “daj im knjige” = “give them the books”)
them.njih: emphatic version of ih, used for emphasis or contrast (e.g. “vidim njih, ne vas”)
them.njima: emphatic or prepositional dative form meaning “to them” or “for them” (e.g. “govorim njima”).

where.gdje: the standard Croatian word for “where” in neutral contexts (e.g. “gdje si?” = “where are you?”)
where.gde: Serbian spelling/pronunciation of gdje, not standard in Croatian
where.kamo: means “to where” or “in what direction” (e.g. “kamo ideš?” = “where are you going?”)
where.odakle: means “from where” (e.g. “odakle dolaziš?” = “where do you come from?”)
where.kuda: used similarly to kamo but often implies a more general route or path (e.g. “kuda prolaziš?”)
where.gđe: an abbreviation for gospođa (Mrs.) and not related to location, often confused due to similar appearance.

there is.ima: commonly used to express “there is” or “there are” in spoken Croatian (e.g. “ima vode” = “there is water”)
there is.postoji: a more formal or literal word meaning “exists” (e.g. “postoji rješenje” = “a solution exists”).

to you.vam: dative plural or formal singular meaning “to you” (e.g. “dajem vam knjigu” = “I’m giving the book to you”)
to you.tebi: informal singular dative form (e.g. “to je za tebi” = “that is for you”).

you know.znaš: informal singular present tense meaning “you know” (e.g. “znaš li ga?” = “do you know him?”)
you know.znate: formal or plural version (e.g. “znate li odgovor?”)
you know.poznaješ: informal singular for “you are familiar with” (e.g. “poznaješ li ovu osobu?” = “do you know this person personally?”)
you know.znas: incorrect/unaccented version of znaš (commonly seen in texting)
you know.poznajete: formal or plural version of poznaješ.

said.rekao: masculine singular past tense of “to say” (e.g. “on je rekao” = “he said”)
said.rekli: plural past form (e.g. “oni su rekli” = “they said”)
said.rečeno: passive past participle meaning “it was said” (e.g. “to je rečeno”)
said.reklo: neuter singular past form, typically used for abstract or impersonal subjects (e.g. “reklo se da dolazi” = “it was said he is coming”).

my.mog: genitive or accusative masculine form used when “my” is the object or after certain prepositions (e.g. “vidim mog brata” = “I see my brother”)
my.mome: dative or locative masculine form (e.g. “pričam mome prijatelju” = “I’m talking to my friend”).

then.onda: the most common word for “then”, meaning “at that time” or “next” (e.g. “onda smo otišli” = “then we left”)
then.tada: formal or slightly more specific word meaning “at that moment” (e.g. “tada sam bio u školi”)
then.zatim: often means “after that” or “and then” in sequences (e.g. “pojeli smo večeru, zatim desert”)
then.potom: a more literary or formal word for “thereafter” or “then” used in writing or speeches.

we will.ćemo: future auxiliary for “we will” placed after the verb (e.g. “napisat ćemo pismo” = “we will write a letter”)
we will.hoćemo: full form meaning “we will” or “we want” (e.g. “hoćemo ići” = “we will go”), cemo and čemo: incorrect or unaccented forms of ćemo, commonly seen in casual typing or texting but not correct in standard Croatian.

to.do: preposition meaning “to” in the sense of reaching a point or destination (e.g. “do kuće” = “to the house”)
to.ka: used to indicate direction “towards” something (e.g. “ka jugu” = “toward the south”), more formal or poetic than prema which is often used instead in modern Croatian.

nothing.ništa: the standard word for “nothing” (e.g. “ne vidim ništa” = “I see nothing”)
nothing.ničega: genitive form meaning “of nothing” (e.g. “bojim se ničega” = “I’m afraid of nothing”)
nothing.nista: unaccented or incorrect version of ništa
nothing.ničeg: shortened or colloquial genitive form, often used in speech (e.g. “nema ničeg tamo” = “there’s nothing there”).

our.nas: accusative form of “us” (not possessive), used when “us” is the object (e.g. “zvali su nas” = “they called us”)
our.naš: masculine singular form of “our” used before masculine nouns (e.g. “naš pas”)
our.naše: neuter or plural form (e.g. “naše dijete” or “naše knjige”)
our.nase: unaccented or informal form of naše, often seen in casual writing or typos.

please.molim: the standard and most common way to say “please” or “you’re welcome” (e.g. “molim vas” = “please”)
please.molimo: formal or plural imperative “we ask”/“please” (e.g. in shops: “izvolite
please.moli: imperative singular “ask” or “please” directed at one person (e.g. “moli ga za pomoć”)
please.molio: past tense masculine form of “asked” (e.g. “molio sam te”)
please.miloga: a poetic or dated genitive form of mil (“dear”), not commonly used for “please” in modern speech, though occasionally seen in phrases like zbog miloga Boga (“for God’s sake”).

say.reći: infinitive form meaning “to say” or “to tell” (e.g. “želim ti nešto reći”)
say.reci: imperative singular (“say!” or “tell!” used to one person)
say.recite: formal or plural imperative (“say” addressed to a group or politely to one person)
say.reči: either a typo of reći or an old spelling still used in Serbian (not standard in Croatian)
say.kaži: synonym for reci, more common in Serbian or regional dialects but still understood in Croatia.

because.jer: the standard word for “because”, used in most spoken and written Croatian (e.g. “kasnim jer je bila gužva”)
because.zato: literally “because of that” or “that’s why”, often used with što (e.g. “zato što je kasnio” = “because he was late”) or alone for emphasis (e.g. “zato sam to učinio” = “that’s why I did it”).

hey.hej: the most common informal way to say “hey” in Croatian (e.g. “hej, što ima?”)
hey.ej: a softer or more casual version of hej, often used to get someone’s attention (e.g. “ej, čekaj!”)
hey.haj: less common, sometimes poetic or used regionally like “come on” (e.g. “haj’mo!” = “let’s go!”).

you can.možeš: informal singular form meaning “you can” (e.g. “možeš mi pomoći?” = “can you help me?”)
you can.možete: formal or plural version (e.g. “možete ući” = “you may enter”)
you can.smijete: means “you are allowed to” (e.g. “smijete li pušiti ovdje?” = “are you allowed to smoke here?”), used when asking about or giving permission.

you will.ćeš: informal singular future tense auxiliary (e.g. “vidjet ćeš” = “you will see”)
you will.hoćeš: full form used for emphasis or in questions (e.g. “hoćeš li doći?” = “will you come?”)
you will.ćete: formal or plural version (e.g. “vi ćete to napraviti”)
you will.hoćete: formal/plural full form (e.g. “hoćete li večerati s nama?”), and ceš, ces
you will.hocete: unaccented or incorrectly spelled versions of ćeš, ćeš, ćete, and hoćete, often found in casual texting but not standard.

us.nam: dative form meaning “to us” (e.g. “dao nam je knjigu” = “he gave us the book”)
us.nama: emphatic or prepositional dative form (e.g. “dao je to nama, ne vama” = “he gave it to us, not to you”).

there.tamo: standard and most common word for “there” in terms of location (e.g. “on je tamo” = “he is there”)
there.ondje: a slightly more formal or poetic synonym for tamo
there.eto: used to point something out that’s nearby or just happened (e.g. “eto ga!” = “there it is!”)
there.eno: used to point at something farther away (e.g. “eno ih!” = “there they are!”)
there.onamo: means “toward there” or “in that direction” (e.g. “idemo onamo”)
there.tede: not a standard Croatian word — likely a typo or dialect word.

people.ljudi: the standard word for “people” (e.g. “dobri ljudi” = “good people”)
people.narod: a more collective or national word for “the people” or “a people” (e.g. “hrvatski narod” = “the Croatian people”)
people.ijudi: not a valid Croatian word — likely a typo for ljudi
people.narode: vocative form used when addressing a people (e.g. “narode moj!” = “my people!”)
people.naroda: genitive form of narod (e.g. “glas naroda” = “voice of the people”)
people.ijude: another likely typo or OCR error for ljude.

you didn't.nisi: informal singular past negative form of “you didn’t” (e.g. “nisi rekao” = “you didn’t say”)
you didn't.niste: formal or plural version (e.g. “niste ništa učinili” = “you didn’t do anything”).

i have to.moram: present tense form meaning “I have to” (e.g. “moram ići” = “I have to go”)
i have to.morat: colloquial shortened future/conditional infinitive form (e.g. “morat ću to napraviti” = “I’ll have to do that”).

always.uvek: Serbian spelling of uvijek, commonly seen but not standard in Croatian
always.uvjek: a common misspelling of uvijek — not correct but often made by learners or in casual writing.

really.stvarno: common and neutral way to say “really” or “truly” (e.g. “stvarno si dobar”)
really.zaista: slightly more formal synonym (e.g. “zaista mi se sviđa”)
really.zbilja: conversational and somewhat emotional version of “really” (e.g. “zbilja to misliš?” = “do you really think that?”)
really.doista: formal or literary alternative for “indeed” or “truly”
really.itekako: emphatic form meaning “very much so” or “definitely” (e.g. “itekako zna što radi”)
really.zbilo: not an adverb — it’s the past form of the verb “zbiti se” (to occur), not used for “really”.

come on.hajde: the standard form for “come on” or “let’s go” (e.g. “hajde
come on.daj: literally means “give” but often used as “come on” in frustration or urging (e.g. “daj, nemoj zezati!”)
come on.ajde: informal or regional variant of hajde (widely used in speech)
come on.ajme: an exclamation of shock, sympathy, or surprise (“oh no”, “oh dear” — e.g. “ajme meni!”), not really the same as “come on” but sometimes emotionally expressive in a similar tone.

one.jedan: masculine nominative form meaning “one” or “a” (e.g. “jedan čovjek” = “one man”)
one.jednog: genitive or accusative masculine form (e.g. “vidim jednog psa”)
one.jedne: genitive feminine form or plural feminine nominative (e.g. “bez jedne greške” or “jedne djevojke”)
one.jedni: masculine plural form meaning “some” or “certain ones” in contrast (e.g. “jedni dolaze, drugi odlaze”)
one.jednim: instrumental masculine or neuter form (e.g. “s jednim prijateljem”)

already.već: the standard word for “already” (e.g. “već sam pojeo” = “I already ate”)
already.ionako: means “anyway” or “in any case,” often implying inevitability (e.g. “ionako nema smisla” = “it doesn’t matter anyway”), not a direct synonym but related in usage tone.

let's go.idemo: the most common phrase for “let’s go” (e.g. “idemo kući” = “let’s go home”)
let's go.hajdemo: more formal or older version of idemo, still correct and used (especially in commands)
let's go.odemo: subjunctive/potential form meaning “that we go” — not used as “let’s go”
let's go.krenemo: means “let’s start” or “let’s set off” (e.g. “krenemo li sada?”)
let's go.ajmo: very common informal/slangy version of idemo, used often in speech
let's go.krenimo: imperative form meaning “let’s begin” or “let’s go” with a sense of initiating movement
let's go.pustimo: means “let us release” or “let go of” — not used for movement
let's go.pođimo: a more literary/formal way to say “let’s go” or “let us depart”.

you think.misliš: informal singular present tense of “you think” (e.g. “što misliš?”)
you think.mislite: formal or plural form (e.g. “što mislite vi?”)
you think.razmišljaš: means “you are thinking” in a more reflective, deliberate way (e.g. “o čemu razmišljaš?” = “what are you thinking about?”)
you think.razmisliš: perfective form meaning “you think it over” (e.g. “razmisliš prije nego odgovoriš”)
you think.pomisliš: sudden or spontaneous thought, often fleeting or emotional (e.g. “što pomisliš kad ga vidiš?”).

won't.neće: the standard future negative form meaning “will not” (e.g. “neće doći” = “he won’t come”)
won't.neče: misspelling of neće, often seen in casual typing or due to keyboard limitations.

things.stvari: the standard plural word for “things” (e.g. “važne stvari” = “important things”)
things.stvarima: the dative/instrumental plural form used for “to the things” or “with the things” (e.g. “bavi se stvarima” = “deals with things”).

time.vrijeme: the standard word for “time” as a concept or weather (e.g. “vrijeme brzo prolazi” = “time goes fast” or “lijepo je vrijeme” = “the weather is nice”)
time.put: means “time” as in “occasion” (e.g. “prvi put” = “the first time”)
time.vremena: genitive form of vrijeme, used in phrases like “nema vremena” = “no time”
time.vreme: Serbian spelling of vrijeme, not standard in Croatian
time.vremenu: dative/locative form (e.g. “u tom vremenu” = “at that time”)
time.vremenski: an adjective meaning “temporal” or “related to time” (e.g. “vremenski okvir” = “time frame”).

mine.moja: feminine singular form of “mine” (e.g. “to je moja torba”)
mine.moje: neuter singular or plural form (e.g. “moje dijete”, “moje stvari”)
mine.mojom: instrumental feminine (e.g. “s mojom prijateljicom”), mojem and mojeg: alternative genitive/dative masculine forms (e.g. “mojeg psa” = “of my dog”)
mine.rudnik: means “mine” in the sense of a mining site — not possessive, so unrelated meaning.

we can.možemo: standard word for “we can” or “we are able to” (e.g. “možemo ići” = “we can go”)
we can.smijemo: means “we are allowed to” or “we may” (e.g. “smijemo li ovdje sjediti?” = “are we allowed to sit here?”).

which.koje: neuter or feminine plural form of “which” (e.g. “koje boje želiš?” = “which color do you want?”)
which.kojoj: dative/locative feminine (e.g. “osobi kojoj vjerujem” = “the person whom I trust”)
which.kojima: dative/instrumental plural (e.g. “ljudima kojima pomažem” = “the people I help”)
which.kojom: instrumental feminine (e.g. “s osobom kojom razgovaram” = “with the person I'm speaking to”)
which.kojih: genitive plural (e.g. “stvari kojih se sjećam” = “things I remember”).

her.joj: dative form meaning “to her” (e.g. “daj joj knjigu” = “give her the book”)
her.ju: short accusative form used after verbs (e.g. “vidim ju” = “I see her”)
her.nju: emphatic accusative form used for contrast or emphasis (e.g. “nju sam vidio, ne tebe”)
her.njom: instrumental form meaning “with her” (e.g. “pričam s njom”)
her.nje: genitive form meaning “of her” (e.g. “bez nje ne mogu” = “I can’t without her”)
her.njoj: emphatic or prepositional dative form (e.g. “dao je to njoj, ne meni”)

they.oni: masculine or mixed-gender plural for “they” (e.g. “oni su došli” = “they came”)
they.one: feminine plural form (e.g. “one su učiteljice” = “they are female teachers”).

you want.želiš: informal singular for “you want” (e.g. “što želiš?” = “what do you want?”)
you want.želite: likely a repeat, but formal/plural again
you want.hoćeš: full form of “you will” or “you want” depending on context (e.g. “hoćeš li ići?”)

evil.žao: does not mean “evil” — it means “sorry” or “sad” (e.g. “žao mi je”)
evil.zlo: the proper word for “evil” as a concept or noun (e.g. “boriti se protiv zla” = “fight against evil”)
evil.zao: masculine adjective meaning “evil” (e.g. “zao čovjek” = “an evil man”)

you have.imaš: informal singular form of “you have” (e.g. “imaš li vremena?” = “do you have time?”)
you have.lmaš: likely a typo for imaš — not a valid word.

of course.naravno: the standard and most common way to say “of course” (e.g. “naravno da dolazim” = “of course I’m coming”)
of course.dakako: a slightly more formal or emphatic synonym, often found in writing or polite conversation (e.g. “Dakako, podržavam to”).

to that.tome: dative form of to, meaning “to that” or “for that” (e.g. “pripadam tome” = “I belong to that”)
to that.tomu: an alternative dative form, a bit more formal or poetic — both tome and tomu are correct and interchangeable in most cases.

could.mogao: masculine singular past/future conditional of “can” (e.g. “mogao sam ići” = “I could have gone”)
could.mogli: masculine plural or mixed-gender plural (e.g. “mogli smo to učiniti”)
could.moglo: neuter form (e.g. “to se moglo izbjeći” = “that could have been avoided”)
could.mogle: feminine plural (e.g. “one su to mogle znati”).

job.posao: the standard noun meaning “job” or “work” (e.g. “imam novi posao”)
job.pošao: NOT the same — it is the past tense of the verb poći meaning “he went” or “he set off” (e.g. “pošao je kući” = “he went home”), so it doesn’t mean “job” despite looking similar.

sir.gospodine: vocative form used when addressing someone directly as “Sir” (e.g. “Izvolite, gospodine” = “Here you go
sir.gospodin: nominative form meaning “gentleman” or “Mr.” (e.g. “Gospodin Novak je stigao”)
sir.ser: not a Croatian word — might be a mix-up with the English “Sir” or the Serbian use in some translations
sir.gospodinu: dative form meaning “to the gentleman” (e.g. “dao sam gospodinu knjigu”)
sir.gospod: archaic or religious form meaning “Lord” (e.g. “Gospod Bog” = “Lord God”), not used for “sir” in daily speech.

means.znači: the standard verb form meaning “means” or “it means” (e.g. “to znači da je gotovo” = “that means it’s over”)
means.znaci: plural of znak meaning “signs” or “symbols” (e.g. “prometni znaci” = “traffic signs”) — not the same as znači
means.sredstva: plural of sredstvo, meaning “means” in the sense of resources or tools (e.g. “prijevozna sredstva” = “means of transport”).

we have.imamo: standard form of “we have” (e.g. “imamo vremena” = “we have time”)
we have.lmamo: a typo or mistyped version of imamo (the “l” is likely a mistaken “i”).

days.dana: genitive plural form meaning “of days” or used to express quantities (e.g. “pet dana” = “five days”)
days.dani: nominative plural meaning “days” as a subject (e.g. “dani su sve duži” = “the days are getting longer”)
days.dane: accusative plural, used when “days” are the object (e.g. “volim sunčane dane” = “I love sunny days”).

never.nikad: informal and commonly used form of “never” (e.g. “nikad nisam bio tamo”)
never.nikada: more formal or emphatic version — both mean the same and are interchangeable depending on tone or emphasis.

day.danu: dative/locative form used in contexts like “on that day” or “to the day” (e.g. “na tom danu” = “on that day”).

were.bili: masculine or mixed-gender plural past tense of “to be” (e.g. “oni su bili sretni” = “they were happy”)
were.bile: feminine plural past tense (e.g. “one su bile tamo” = “they were [feminine] there”).

works.radi: third person singular of “raditi” meaning “he/she/it works” or “is working” (e.g. “on radi svaki dan” = “he works every day”)
works.djela: plural of djelo, meaning “works” in the sense of creations, deeds, or acts (e.g. “njegova djela su poznata” = “his works are well-known”) — not to be confused with the verb raditi.

year.god: a shortened or poetic form of godina (rarely used in modern Croatian except in expressions like “sto god”)
year.godine: plural or genitive form (e.g. “tri godine” = “three years” or “kroz godine” = “over the years”)
year.godinu: accusative singular (e.g. “čekam jednu godinu” = “I’ve been waiting one year”).

better.bolje: comparative adverb meaning “better” in the sense of “in a better way” or “more well” (e.g. “osjećam se bolje”)
better.bolji: masculine comparative adjective (e.g. “bolji rezultat” = “a better result”)
better.boljim: instrumental or dative masculine/neuter form (e.g. “s boljim timom” = “with a better team”).

own.svoje: reflexive possessive used with plural or neuter nouns (e.g. “uzmi svoje stvari” = “take your own things”)
own.vlastiti: masculine singular adjective meaning “own” (e.g. “vlastiti stan” = “one’s own apartment”)
own.vlastite: feminine plural or accusative (e.g. “vlastite ideje” = “your own ideas”)
own.vlastitim: dative/instrumental plural (e.g. “s vlastitim riječima” = “with your own words”)
own.vlastitog: genitive masculine (e.g. “bez vlastitog mišljenja” = “without your own opinion”)
own.svojem: alternate dative/locative of svoj (e.g. “u svojem stilu”)

you have to.moraš: informal singular form meaning “you have to” or “you must” (e.g. “moraš učiti” = “you have to study”)
you have to.morate: formal or plural version (e.g. “morate poštovati pravila” = “you must follow the rules”)
you have to.moras: unaccented or misspelled form of moraš, common in casual texting but incorrect in standard Croatian.

don't.nemoj: imperative singular form meaning “don’t” used to tell one person not to do something (e.g. “nemoj to raditi” = “don’t do that”)
don't.nemojte: formal or plural version used when addressing more than one person or politely (e.g. “nemojte zaboraviti” = “don’t forget”).

god.bože: vocative form used when calling out to God (e.g. “Bože, pomozi mi!” = “God, help me!”)
god.bog: nominative form, the standard word for “God” or “god” (e.g. “Bog je stvorio svijet”)
god.boga: accusative/genitive form (e.g. “vidim boga” or “strah od boga” = “fear of God”)
god.bogu: dative form (e.g. “molim se bogu” = “I pray to God”)
god.božje: neuter possessive form meaning “God’s” (e.g. “Božje ime” = “God’s name”).

i won't.neću: standard future negative of “I will not” (e.g. “neću to napraviti” = “I won’t do it”)
i won't.neču: incorrect spelling of neću, often seen in casual typing but not correct in formal use.

someone.netko: the standard word for “someone” (e.g. “netko kuca na vrata” = “someone is knocking”)
someone.nekoga: genitive/accusative form meaning “someone” as the object (e.g. “vidim nekoga”)
someone.nekog: shortened or informal genitive/accusative of netko, used in speech (e.g. “tražim nekog”)
someone.nekoj: dative feminine form (e.g. “pričam nekoj djevojci” = “I’m talking to some girl”).

code.kod: typically means “code” as in a password or symbol system, but also used as a preposition meaning “at someone’s place” (e.g. “kod kuće” = “at home”), so context matters; šifru: accusative form of šifra, meaning a secret code or password (e.g. “unesi šifru” = “enter the password”).

thought.mislio: masculine singular past tense of “thought” (e.g. “mislio sam da znaš” = “I thought you knew”)
thought.pomislio: masculine form of “had a sudden thought” (e.g. “pomislio sam nešto čudno” = “I suddenly thought something odd”)
thought.pomislili: plural of pomislio, used when a group suddenly thought of something.

see.vidjeti: the infinitive “to see” (e.g. “želim te vidjeti” = “I want to see you”)
see.vidjet: shortened conversational form of vidjeti, used frequently in speech but not formal writing
see.vide: third person plural form meaning “they see” (e.g. “oni te vide”).

mom.mama: standard word for “mom” (e.g. “moja mama je kod kuće”)
mom.mamu: accusative form, used when mom is the object (e.g. “vidim mamu” = “I see mom”)
mom.mamom: instrumental form, used for “with mom” (e.g. “idem s mamom” = “I’m going with mom”).

looks like.izgleda: the most common way to say “looks like” (e.g. “izgleda umorno” = “he/she looks tired”)
looks like.liči: informal or colloquial for “resembles” (e.g. “liči na oca” = “looks like his dad”)
looks like.sliči: more formal/literary synonym of liči, meaning “resembles” or “is similar to” (e.g. “sliči majci”).

two.dvoje: collective or mixed-gender form used when referring to a pair or couple (e.g. “dvoje djece” = “two children”)
two.dvojica: masculine collective, often used for two males acting together (e.g. “dvojica policajaca”)
two.dve: Serbian or dialectal version of dvije — not standard in Croatian
two.dvojice: genitive of dvojica (e.g. “jednog od dvojice” = “one of the two men”).

had.imao: masculine singular past tense of “to have” (e.g. “imao sam psa” = “I had a dog”)
had.imali: masculine or mixed-gender plural (e.g. “imali smo vremena”)

life.život: nominative form, the base word meaning “life” (e.g. “život je lijep”)
life.života: genitive form used for possession or after certain verbs (e.g. “kraj života” = “end of life”)
life.zivot: a typo or unaccented version of život.

dad.tata: nominative form of “dad” (e.g. “tata je u kući”)
dad.tati: dative form (e.g. “daj tati” = “give it to dad”)

you work.radiš: informal singular present tense of “you work” (e.g. “gdje radiš?” = “where do you work?”)
you work.radite: formal or plural form (e.g. “što radite vi?”)
you work.radis: unaccented or misspelled form of radiš, often seen in casual typing.

saw.vidio: masculine singular past tense of “saw” (e.g. “vidio sam te jučer” = “I saw you yesterday”)
saw.vidjeli: masculine or mixed-gender plural (e.g. “vidjeli smo film”)
saw.videli: Serbian spelling of vidjeli, not standard in Croatian
saw.viđao: masculine imperfect past tense meaning “used to see repeatedly” (e.g. “često sam ga viđao”)
saw.ugledao: masculine past tense of “caught sight of” or “spotted” (e.g. “ugledao sam pticu” = “I spotted a bird”).

very.jako: the most common and versatile word for “very” or “strongly” (e.g. “jako dobar” = “very good”)
very.vrlo: a slightly more formal or literary synonym for “very” (e.g. “vrlo važan sastanak”)
very.veoma: similar to vrlo, also formal and used more in writing or polite speech (e.g. “veoma lijep dan”).

help.pomoći: infinitive form “to help” (e.g. “želim ti pomoći” = “I want to help you”)
help.pomoć: noun form meaning “help” as a concept (e.g. “trebam pomoć” = “I need help”)
help.pomogne: third-person singular present/future subjunctive (e.g. “ako mi pomogne”)
help.upomoć: a cry for help (“help!” like yelling in trouble)
help.pomagati: imperfective form meaning “to be helping” or “to help regularly” (e.g. “voli pomagati drugima”)
help.pomognete: formal/plural present/future subjunctive (e.g. “nadam se da pomognete”)
help.pomoči: misspelling or dialectal of pomoći, not standard.

go.kreni: informal imperative meaning “start” or “set off” (e.g. “kreni već jednom!”)
go.poći: infinitive meaning “to set off” or “to go” in a more formal/literary sense (e.g. “moramo poći”)
go.krene: third person singular subjunctive (e.g. “kad krene, nema stajanja”)
go.krenu: third person plural (e.g. “krenu zajedno” = “they start off”)

i see.vidim: present tense, “I see” (e.g. “vidim te” = “I see you”)
i see.viđam: imperfective, meaning “I see (repeatedly, regularly)” (e.g. “viđam ga svaki tjedan” = “I see him every week”).

home.kući: locative form of kuća, used to mean “at home” (e.g. “sam kod kući” = “I’m at home”)
home.dom: formal word meaning “home” as an institution or concept (e.g. “dom za starije” = “retirement home”)
home.domu: dative/locative form of dom (e.g. “vraćam se domu”)

knows.zna: present tense of “to know” in general or factual terms (e.g. “on zna istinu” = “he knows the truth”)
knows.poznaje: means “is familiar with” or “knows personally” (e.g. “poznaje tog čovjeka” = “he knows that man”).

should have.trebao: masculine form meaning “should have” (e.g. “trebao sam doći” = “I should have come”)
should have.trebalo: neuter form (e.g. “to se trebalo dogoditi” = “that should have happened”)

happened.dogodilo: neuter past form of “it happened” (e.g. “što se dogodilo?”)
happened.desilo: synonym for dogodilo, used more in Serbian or Bosnian speech
happened.događalo: imperfect past tense meaning “was happening” (e.g. “to se događalo više puta”).

again.opet: the most common and informal word for “again” (e.g. “opet kasniš” = “you’re late again”)
again.ponovo: similar to ponovno, more common in Serbian but still understood in Croatian
again.iznova: emphasizes starting from scratch or doing over completely (e.g. “počnimo iznova” = “let’s start over”).

just.upravo: means “just now” or “exactly” (e.g. “upravo sam stigao” = “I just arrived”)
just.maloprije: means “a little earlier” or “just before now” (e.g. “bio je ovdje maloprije” = “he was here just a moment ago”).

make.učiniti: a formal or abstract verb meaning “to do” or “to make happen” (e.g. “želim učiniti nešto dobro” = “I want to do something good”)
make.napraviti: common, practical verb for “to make” or “to build” something tangible (e.g. “napraviti kolač” = “make a cake”)
make.napravit: informal/future-shortened form of napraviti, used in speech (e.g. “napravit ću to kasnije”)
make.natjerati: means “to force” or “to make someone do something” (e.g. “natjerao me da priznam”)
make.praviti: imperfective form meaning “to be making” or “to make regularly” (e.g. “pravim planove” = “I’m making plans”).

after.nakon: standard word for “after” followed by a noun (e.g. “nakon škole” = “after school”)
after.poslije: interchangeable with nakon, used both with nouns and on its own (e.g. “vidimo se poslije” = “see you later”)
after.posle: Serbian or dialectal variant of poslije, not standard in Croatian.

immediately.odmah: the most common and neutral word for “immediately” (e.g. “odmah dolazim” = “I’m coming right away”)
immediately.smjesta: a more urgent or forceful synonym meaning “right this instant” or “at once” (e.g. “napusti prostoriju smjesta!” = “leave the room immediately!”).

name.ime: the standard word for “name” (e.g. “moje ime je Ana”)
name.imenu: dative/locative form (e.g. “posvećeno njegovom imenu” = “dedicated to his name”)
name.naziv: means “name” in the sense of a title or label for things, not people (e.g. “naziv knjige” = “the title of the book”).

certainly.sigurno: commonly used to mean “certainly” or “surely,” often with a tone of confidence or reassurance (e.g. “sigurno će doći” = “he’ll certainly come”)
certainly.svakako: means “certainly” or “by all means,” and is also used for agreement (e.g. “svakako, to je dobra ideja” = “certainly, that’s a good idea”)
certainly.zacijelo: a slightly more formal or literary synonym of sigurno, meaning “undoubtedly” or “surely.”

three.troje: collective form used when referring to a group as a unit, especially when mixed-gender or when referring to children or people without specifying gender (e.g. “troje djece” = “three children”)
three.trojica: masculine collective form, used specifically for groups of three men or masculine figures (e.g. “trojica prijatelja” = “three (male) friends”).

i'm going.idem: present tense “I’m going” in the sense of physically heading somewhere (e.g. “idem kući” = “I’m going home”)
i'm going.krenem: perfective form meaning “I set off” or “I begin to go,” often used in future or conditional phrases (e.g. “kad krenem, javit ću ti” = “when I go/set off, I’ll let you know”).

nobody.nitko: standard word for “nobody” (e.g. “nitko nije došao” = “nobody came”)
nobody.nikog: genitive/accusative form of nitko (e.g. “ne vidim nikog” = “I don’t see anyone”)
nobody.nikom: dative form of nitko, meaning “to nobody” (e.g. “nikom ne vjerujem” = “I trust no one”).

man.čovjek: the standard and most general word for “man” or “human being” (e.g. “dobar čovjek” = “a good man”)
man.čovječe: vocative form, used like “man!” or “dude!” as an exclamation (e.g. “pa čovječe!” = “come on
man.muškarac: refers specifically to a male, rather than a general “person” (e.g. “on je muškarac” = “he is a man”), čovek, čoveče, čoveka, covek
man.čovjeće: all either Serbian spellings (čovek, čoveče, čoveka) or typos/misspellings of Croatian čovjek and čovječe.

many.mnogo: general word for “many” or “a lot,” used with both countable and uncountable nouns (e.g. “mnogo ljudi” = “many people”)
many.mnogi: masculine plural meaning “many” as a subject (e.g. “mnogi su došli” = “many came”)
many.mnogih: genitive plural (e.g. “priče mnogih ljudi” = “the stories of many people”).

team.tim: the standard word for “team” (e.g. “naš tim je spreman” = “our team is ready”)
team.ekipa: informal or casual synonym, can also mean “crew” or “group of friends” (e.g. “super ekipa!” = “great group!”)
team.tima: genitive form of tim (e.g. “član tima” = “team member”)
team.momčad: older or more formal term, commonly used in sports (e.g. “nogometna momčad” = “football team”).

which one.koju: accusative feminine singular of “which” (e.g. “koju knjigu želiš?” = “which book do you want?”)
which one.kojeg: genitive or accusative masculine singular (e.g. “kojeg čovjeka si vidio?” = “which man did you see?”)
which one.kojega: full, more formal version of kojeg — they’re interchangeable in meaning, with kojega more common in written or careful speech.

hello.zdravo: a standard and friendly way to say “hello” (used similarly to “hi”), appropriate in both formal and informal settings, especially common in the Balkans.

about.oko: means “about” when estimating or approximating (e.g. “oko deset sati” = “about ten o’clock”), but also means “around” in a spatial sense (e.g. “oko kuće” = “around the house”)
about.otprilike: means “approximately” or “roughly” (e.g. “otprilike 20 ljudi” = “about 20 people”), used mainly with numbers and quantities.
